verified_claim: Pease et al. explain that TBI is an initiating insult that can produce structural brain injury and trigger epileptogenesis. During the subsequent latent period, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, neuronal injury and altered signaling can contribute to the structural reorganization of neural circuitry and formation of epileptogenic networks.
limitation_note: The source establishes a possible post-traumatic mechanism rather than inevitable epileptogenesis after every TBI. Many injured individuals do not develop epilepsy. Several molecular mechanisms are supported mainly by preclinical models, and their individual causal contributions in humans remain incompletely validated.

verified_claim: The review explains that traumatic injury-associated neuronal loss, gliosis, neuroinflammation and abnormal neural circuit reorganization can promote epileptogenesis. Altered excitation-inhibition balance and recurrent excitatory connections can increase susceptibility to spontaneous recurrent seizures. Post-traumatic epilepsy is distinguished from acute provoked seizures by delayed unprovoked seizure occurrence and high recurrence risk.
limitation_note: The mechanisms increase susceptibility but do not guarantee PTE. Evidence for specific cellular remodeling pathways is partly derived from animal studies and may not be fully established in humans. Early provoked post-traumatic seizures within seven days should not be treated as equivalent to later unprovoked seizures or established PTE. Not every structural brain lesion becomes epileptogenic.
